gap: No result ChatGPT got states how much current each charger pulls from the 12 V socket at full load against the 10 A / 120 W limit most owner's manuals set: Anker 535 is rated 7.2 A in, Anker Nano 75W 8 A in, UGREEN 145W 17.8 A in, and the Anker 167.5W needs at least 14.0 A before losses, so the two high-power picks cannot reach rated output through a 10 A socket.
standout_why: Soldermag (opened) gives no socket amperage, fuse limit, input current or price for any pick. ChatGPT's own answer says 'provided your car socket supports the load' with no number. Wired (cited) and thisUSB could not be opened (fetch blocked / TLS error), so I cannot confirm they lack it; a Wired text grep was not possible. Anker's own 535 page (opened) also shows the two-device split is 9 W + 9 W on USB-C2 + USB-A, which neither ChatGPT nor Soldermag's main text states for two devices.
decides: For a car whose manual caps the socket at 120 W / 10 A (Mazda CX-90 wording; 2011 Toyota RAV4 'less than 10 A'), the Anker Nano 75W retractable (8 A rated input, 80% of fuse) is the highest-output pick that fits; the Anker 535 (7.2 A, 72%) also fits but drops to 9 W per port when its USB-C2 and USB-A are both used. The UGREEN 145W (17.8 A max input, 178% of a 10 A fuse, 119% of 15 A) and Anker 167.5W (167.5 W / 12 V = 14.0 A minimum before conversion loss) only make sense on a 20 A socket, which undercuts ChatGPT's 'best high power' pick for ordinary cars. On $/W the Nano 75W is $0.40/W vs Belkin 42W $0.59/W.

findings.note: Anker: 'When using both the USB-C 2 and USB-A ports at the same time, the maximum power output for each port is 9W.' Three devices: USB-C1 45 W. Single USB-C max 20 V⎓3.35 A = 67 W.
